chapters.title: Chapter 5: Signal Research and Alpha Construction

lessons.title: Combining Alternative Data with Traditional Factors

body.text: An alternative data signal rarely needs to beat a traditional factor. It needs to disagree with one often enough to be worth combining with it.

children.text: Most alternative data signals, honestly evaluated with the tools from the last lesson, land in the modest 0.02 to 0.05 IC range, not the standalone blockbuster range. That is not a failure. This lesson shows how a modest, genuinely independent signal combined properly with established traditional factors can be worth more than either one used alone, and why combining two similar signals barely helps at all.
The Orthogonality Check: Correlation Before Combination

markDefs.definition: How independent two signals are from each other, typically measured as the correlation between their cross-sectional rankings or their IC time series. A genuinely orthogonal signal adds new information when combined with another; a highly correlated one mostly just adds noise to a signal you already had.

children.text: Before combining any alt data signal with an existing factor, check their

. A web-traffic-based signal that mostly tracks the same thing price momentum already captures adds little value once combined, no matter how good its standalone IC looked, because you are effectively just adding a noisier copy of a factor you already use. The whole payoff of alternative data comes from finding a signal that disagrees with your existing factors often enough to be worth its own weight in the blend.

body.caption: How alt data categories from Chapter 2 typically relate to traditional factors

cells: Value (P/E, P/B based)
How cheap a stock is relative to its reported fundamentals
Usually low overlap with transaction, satellite, or supply chain data, which measure current activity rather than historical accounting ratios
Price momentum
Recent trend in the stock price itself
Higher overlap risk with web traffic or search trend signals if those signals mostly move alongside sentiment that is already pushing the price
Quality (ROE, margin stability)
Business and balance sheet quality from reported financials
Usually low overlap, since it is backward-looking and accounting-based, unlike most alt data's forward-looking, activity-based nature
Size or low volatility
Market capitalization or historical return volatility
Generally low overlap, though smaller companies may simply have thinner alt data coverage to begin with

children.text: The Payoff of Combining Uncorrelated Signals: A Worked Example

Because ICIR behaves like a Sharpe ratio for a signal, as established in the previous lesson, combining two signals follows the exact same math used to combine two imperfectly correlated return streams into a portfolio.

body.caption: For two signals with equal individual ICIR, combined with equal weights, where rho is the correlation between the two signals. Lower correlation produces a larger boost from combining them.

body.title: Combine Two Near-Orthogonal Signals
body.prompt: A traditional Value composite and a new alt-data signal each have an ICIR of 0.5, matching the ICIR calculated in the previous lesson. The correlation between the two signals is a low 0.1. Using ICIR_combined = ICIR x sqrt(2 / (1 + rho)), what is the combined ICIR, to two decimal places?
body.explanation: ICIR_combined = 0.5 x sqrt(2 / 1.1) = 0.5 x sqrt(1.818) = 0.5 x 1.348 = 0.674, which rounds to 0.67. Combining these two low-correlation, equally strong signals produced a combined ICIR noticeably higher than either signal's individual 0.5, purely from the diversification benefit of low correlation, without either signal itself getting any better.

body.title: What if the Two Signals Were Highly Correlated Instead?
body.question: Using the same formula and the same individual ICIR of 0.5 each, but with a correlation of 0.8 between the two signals instead of 0.1, the combined ICIR works out to about 0.53, barely above the individual 0.5. What does this contrast with the previous exercise's result of 0.67 demonstrate?
options: Combining signals never actually helps, so it isn't worth the effort
The correlation between two signals matters more to the combination's payoff than either signal's individual strength
A correlation of 0.8 means the second signal is actively harmful and should be discarded
This formula only applies to alternative data, not to traditional factors
body.explanation: Both scenarios started from the exact same individual ICIR of 0.5 for each signal, only the correlation between them changed, and that single change moved the combined result from 0.67 down to about 0.53. This is precisely why the orthogonality check earlier in this lesson matters more, in practice, than chasing a slightly higher standalone IC: a genuinely independent, modest signal is worth far more in combination than a strong but redundant one.

body.caption: Four ways to actually combine signals, from simplest to most complex

cells: Equal-weighted z-score average
Cross-sectionally z-score each signal, then average them with equal weights
Simple and robust, but ignores that some signals are more reliable than others
ICIR-weighted blend
Weight each signal's z-score in proportion to its own ICIR, giving more weight to more consistent signals
Requires enough history to estimate ICIR reliably in the first place
Two-stage or conditional application
Use traditional factors to define a base tilt or shortlist, then apply the alt data signal only within that narrower set
Useful when the alt data signal is a timing overlay rather than a standalone ranking across the full universe
Machine learning-based combination
A regression or tree-based model learns a potentially nonlinear combination of multiple signals
Carries real overfitting risk, especially with a modest number of alt data history points, a topic Chapter 6 covers directly

children.text: Weighting by Confidence: An ICIR-Weighted Blend

A simple, defensible starting point for weighting is to give each signal a share of the blend proportional to its own ICIR, so a more consistent signal earns more influence over the final ranking than a noisier one, without requiring the full covariance-matrix optimization that a formally optimal combination would need.

body.title: Calculate an ICIR-Proportional Weight
body.prompt: A traditional Value composite has an ICIR of 0.6, and a new alt-data signal has an ICIR of 0.3. In a simple ICIR-proportional blend, what weight, as a percentage, should the alt-data signal receive?
body.explanation: Weight = alt-data ICIR / (Value ICIR + alt-data ICIR) = 0.3 / (0.6 + 0.3) = 0.3 / 0.9 = 0.333, or 33.3%. The more established Value composite, with double the ICIR, earns roughly double the weight of the newer alt-data signal, a sensible starting point that still gives the newer signal a meaningful say in the final ranking rather than either ignoring it or over-trusting it.

body.title: Why this isn't the mathematically optimal combination

children.text: A formally optimal combination of many signals requires their full covariance matrix, not just each signal's own ICIR in isolation, since two signals that individually look reasonable can still be poor complements if their errors are correlated in a way a simple ICIR-proportional weight cannot see. That full optimization is a genuine portfolio construction topic beyond this course's scope. The ICIR-weighted blend here is a practical, honest starting point precisely because it is simple enough to reason about and hard to badly misuse, not because it is the theoretical optimum.

body.text: Before reaching for a fancier combination method, check correlation first. A simple equal-weighted average of two genuinely orthogonal, modest signals will usually beat a sophisticated combination of two redundant ones.
The signal strengths, correlations, and weights used in this lesson are illustrative teaching examples, not results for any real strategy. Nothing here is a recommendation to trade any security.

points: Most alt data signals land in a modest standalone IC range, which is fine, because the real payoff usually comes from combining them well, not from any single signal being a blockbuster on its own
Check correlation with existing traditional factors before combining, a highly correlated alt data signal adds little value regardless of how good its standalone IC looks

Because ICIR behaves like a Sharpe ratio for a signal, combining two signals follows the same math as combining two imperfectly correlated return streams: ICIR_combined = ICIR x sqrt(2 / (1 + correlation))
Low correlation between two equally strong signals produces a meaningfully larger combined ICIR than high correlation does, even with identical individual signal strength

Common combination methods range from a simple equal-weighted z-score average to ICIR-weighted blends, two-stage conditional application, and machine learning combinations, each with its own trade-offs
An ICIR-proportional weighting is a practical, defensible starting point, not the mathematically optimal combination, which would require the full covariance structure across signals
